title: Multi-class: one-vs-rest & softmax
intro: More than two classes? scikit-learn handles that automatically — but there is a choice happening behind the scenes: separate binary classifiers per class (one-vs-rest), or one joint model with a softmax loss. The consequences are small but understandable.

blocks.html: So far all the conceptual stories were binary (2 classes), while all along we were simply doing multi-class classification with the wine dataset (3 classes). Time to lift the curtain: how do linear classifiers pull that off? There are two popular strategies.

One-vs-rest trains a dedicated binary classifier for every class. The code y == 0 returns an array that is True wherever y equals 0 — so the first classifier learns "class 0 or not-0", the second "1 or not-1", and so on. Predicting is then done by letting all classifiers compute their raw model output (in scikit-learn: decision_function): the class with the largest raw output wins — that classifier is the most convinced. In the course, classifier 0 wins, so you predict class 0.

blocks.caption: Rebuilding one-vs-rest by hand
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)

# Three binary classifiers: 'class 0 or not', 'class 1 or not', ...
clfs = [LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(X, y == c) for c in (0, 1, 2)]

i = 0
raw = [clf.decision_function([X[i]])[0] for clf in clfs]
print('Raw outputs per classifier:', np.round(raw, 2))
print('Manual OvR prediction     :', int(np.argmax(raw)),
      '(largest raw output)')

blocks.html: What makes OvR attractive: you simply reuse your existing binary classifier implementation — nothing new is needed. scikit-learn does this, among others, via the liblinear solver.

The multinomial approach instead adapts the loss function so that it directly optimises the multi-class problem — terms you will encounter: multinomial logistic regression, softmax, or cross-entropy loss. You fit once for all classes instead of separately per class. In the world of neural networks this is the standard. Both strategies can also output probabilities, just like a binary classifier.

blocks.label: softmax
blocks.latex: \hat{p}_k \;=\; \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}}, \qquad z_k = \text{raw output for class } k
blocks.caption: The generalised sigmoid for K classes: all probabilities are positive and sum to 1.

rows: loss is closer to accuracy — sometimes a better score

sections.title: What do the coefficients look like?

blocks.html: In the binary case you had one coefficient per feature plus one intercept. For 3 classes with OvR you have 3 whole binary classifiers: so one coefficient per feature per class, and one intercept per class. On the wine dataset (13 features), coef_ is therefore a 3×13 array. The multinomial version learns exactly as many parameters (also 3×13) — the approach differs, but broadly the parameters have the same interpretations.

blocks.caption: Comparing coefficient shapes
blocks.source:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# liblinear does one-vs-rest; lbfgs (default) does multinomial
ovr = LogisticRegression(solver='liblinear', max_iter=5000).fit(X, y)
multi = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(X, y)

print('OvR         coef_:', ovr.coef_.shape, ' intercept_:', ovr.intercept_.shape)
print('Multinomial coef_:', multi.coef_.shape, ' intercept_:', multi.intercept_.shape)
print('OvR predicts        :', ovr.predict([X[0]])[0])
print('Multinomial predicts:', multi.predict([X[0]])[0])
